prime.problem: You tell an agent something durable (edit USER.md, save a memory, add a rule) and it keeps acting as if you hadn't. The write succeeded; the model just never saw it. Without a model of when a write reaches a request, you debug prompt compliance when the real fault is a stale copy.
prime.fits: The previous card showed that the working set is assembled for each call. This card asks how often the assembler rereads its sources, and what caching and reproducibility cost you if it rereads too often. The next card, compaction, turns out to be one of the moments the snapshot refreshes.
expect: snapshot cache vs provider cache hit
prime.goal: Given a harness and a durable write, say which call first carries the new value, what that refresh costs in cache misses, and which stale copies are left behind in history.

attend: In the AMBER/COBALT test, why does an unchanged system-prompt digest prove the file edit never reached the model?
Why does compaction make a cheap moment to rebuild the snapshot, compared with an arbitrary turn?
A per-turn rebuild with no clock costs 39,000 prefilled tokens but one with a timestamp costs 125,400. What single design choice causes the gap?
After the Tuesday run's refresh at call 7, which copy of the truth is still wrong, and why doesn't the refresh fix it?
Why did Govindarajan keep the prompt digest and the provider's cached-token count as two separate metrics?

must: The runtime builds the system prompt once and reuses it → a write to USER.md changes the disk but not the next request → the model keeps the old value until a refresh boundary (a new session, or compaction in Hermes) rebuilds the snapshot

Provider caches reuse the longest unchanged prefix → any changed byte in the system prompt invalidates everything after it → rebuilding every turn is only as cheap as the prompt's least stable byte (a clock makes every call a full miss)

Compaction rewrites history anyway → everything after the system prompt is a cache miss at that call regardless → rebuilding the snapshot there costs only the system prompt's own tokens, not the whole history behind it, which is why it is a natural refresh point

Refreshing puts the new value in the request → but summaries, tool results and earlier replies still hold the old value or decisions made under it → refreshing a fact and reconciling its stale copies in history are separate jobs
elevated: Inject-on-change appends a note at the tail → the cached prefix survives (33,650 vs 33,600 tokens in the Tuesday run) → but the old value stays in the snapshot, so the model sees two conflicting copies

A cached prompt object and a provider cache hit are different caches → an unchanged digest says the runtime didn't rebuild, not that the provider served from cache → you need both metrics to debug either
reference: Hermes's three prompt tiers (stable, context, volatile) and which files sit in each
marker words AMBER and COBALT; 22 calls, 16 turns, 2 sessions
the illustrative sizes in the simulation (10,000 / 1,800 / 1,000 / 50)

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the four states a value passes through, from file to model, and mark where a snapshot sits and what moves it. Then, in 3–4 sentences, explain why a harness would choose to let the model see stale data.
checklist: durable source → cached prompt snapshot → selected live history → provider-bound request
a write changes the source; only a refresh boundary (new session, compaction) changes the snapshot
the snapshot keeps prompt bytes stable → cacheable, reproducible, no change under an in-flight request
per-turn rebuild breaks the cache whenever any byte changes
refresh ≠ reconcile: stale copies in history survive a refresh
a write receipt should say both whether the source changed and when the model will see it

retrieve.q: Explain to a teammate why "I updated USER.md and the agent ignored it" is usually not a model-compliance problem in Hermes v0.20.1.
answer: USER.md is an input to a session-level snapshot, not a live lookup
the next request still carried the old profile; the prompt digest was unchanged
the fix is a refresh boundary (new session, or compression for memory and profile), not a stronger instruction

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to the Tuesday run's new USER.md rule under a snapshot-per-session harness, call by call, from the edit after step 4 to call 9.
answer: calls 5 and 6 still carry the old snapshot and hit the provider cache
compaction before call 7 rebuilds the prompt with the rule and writes the summary
calls 7–9 carry the rule, but also the summary "tests passing"
the rule arrives two calls late, and the stale claim is not corrected

retrieve.q: You must choose a refresh policy for an agent whose memory changes a few times a session. Compare snapshot-per-session, per-turn rebuild and inject-on-change on freshness, cache cost and the risk each one carries.
answer: snapshot: cheapest and stable, but lagged until the next boundary
per-turn rebuild: fresh next call, one full re-prefill per change, a full miss every call if anything volatile like a clock is in the prompt
inject-on-change: fresh and cache-cheap, but leaves two conflicting copies
pick by how urgent the fact is: a revocation can't wait; a profile tweak can

retrieve.q: A dashboard shows the system-prompt digest unchanged between two calls. What can you conclude, and what can't you?
answer: you can conclude the runtime didn't rebuild the prompt
you can't conclude the provider served it from cache: check cache-read tokens in usage metadata
Hermes showed 0 cached tokens on fresh sessions and 15,872 on repeats, a separate signal

compare.q: The prompt-caching card treats a stable prefix as a speed win. This card treats it as a freshness cost. What is the one mechanism behind both, and when does the freshness cost win the argument?
answer: the same thing: reuse requires identical leading bytes
speed side: unchanged bytes skip prefill
freshness side: unchanged bytes mean new facts can't enter the prefix
freshness wins when a fact must act now (revocation, stop), so you pay the miss or inject at the tail

compare.q: That card says put stable parts first and changes last. Where does a profile file like USER.md belong under that rule, and what does Hermes's choice to snapshot it reveal about how "stable" is decided?
answer: Hermes places it in the volatile tier, near the end of the system prompt
stability is decided by lifecycle (how often it changes per session), not by importance
snapshotting turns a volatile source into stable bytes for the session, trading freshness for cache and reproducibility

predict.q: A harness snapshots per session, and a subagent is spawned at call 6 of the Tuesday run, after the USER.md edit. Does the subagent see the new rule? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Not knowable from the parent's snapshot alone. In Hermes v0.20.1 a delegated child gets a separately constructed prompt, not the parent's copy, so if that construction rereads USER.md the child sees the new rule while the parent still doesn't. Two contexts in one run can then disagree. The post defers the details to Part 4; treat it as something to test, not assume.

apply.done: Your rerun shows snapshot and no-clock rebuild both first seeing the edit at step 7, with the same 33,600 prefilled tokens: the edit and the refresh boundary coincide, so the snapshot loses nothing.
